overview.description: RÃºssi (Icelandic for 'Russian') is a unique and strategic two-player variation of Whist played in Iceland. It distinguishes itself from standard 'Russian Whist' (Vint) by its hybrid layout: players have cards in their hand AND a collection of face-up and face-down cards on the table. It is a game of information asymmetry, where winning depends on managing visible threats and uncovering your own hidden resources.

history.origins: Likely derived from Scandinavian Whist variants that were imported to Iceland in the late 19th/early 20th century. The name 'RÃºssi' is somewhat mysterious but common in Icelandic folk games.
timeline: 1900s: Traditional 'RÃºssi' becomes a common pastime in Icelandic fishing villages.
1970s: Formalized in Icelandic card game collections.
Present: Remains a popular 'Patience-style' competitive game for two people.
history.evolution: The game's layout (half hidden, half visible) is likely an evolution of solitaire games adapted for head-to-head play.
history.cultural: In Iceland, RÃºssi is often played during long winter evenings when only two players are available.

setup.players: Two players only. A standard 52-card pack is used; cards in each suit rank A (high) down to 2 (low). Turn to deal alternates; each player receives 26 cards: 9 face down on the table, 9 face up on those, and 8 in hand.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card pack; A (high) to 2 (low) in each suit.
setup.dealing: Turn to deal alternates. Each player receives 26 cards: 9 face down on table (5 lower row, 4 upper row), then 9 face up on top of those, then 8 to hand. Dealer's opponent receives first card; cards dealt alternately.

rules.objective: The objective is to win more tricks than the opponent. There are 26 tricks in total; the player who wins the majority wins the game. There is no point scoring.
rules.gameplay: Two players; deal alternates. Each player gets 26 cards: 9 face down on table (5+4 rows), 9 face up on top, 8 in hand. Non-dealer leads. Each trick is two cards; play from hand or face-up layout; when a layout card is played the card beneath is turned face up. Must follow suit if possible. No trumps. Higher card of led suit wins; trick winner leads next. Player with more tricks wins.
keyRules: Must follow suit if possible from hand or face-up layout.
No trumps; highest card of led suit wins the trick.
Trick winner leads to the next trick.

strategy.basic: Table Conservation. Don't play your hand cards early. Your hand is your 'Secret Weapon' because your opponent cannot see them. Use the table cards to follow suit whenever possible. If you can win a trick with a table card, do soâ€”save your hand for when you need to surprise the opponent or win a critical lead.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Uncovering' Priority: Prioritize playing table cards that uncover face-down cards. The more face-up cards you have, the more flexibility you have to follow suit. If you have only one card of a suit on the table, and it's face-up, guard itâ€”if you play it and uncover a face-down card of a different suit, you might leave yourself 'Void' and vulnerable.
strategy.advanced: Defensive Lead-Blocking: If you see your opponent has a King of Spades face-up on the table, and you have the Ace in your hand, don't lead Spades yourself. Wait for them to lead it, or wait until you can lead a different suit that forces them to play their King. Since there are no trumps, 'Controlling the Lead' is everything.
tips: Pay attention to which face-down cards are uncovered. Information is your most valuable asset.
If you have no cards of a suit in your hand OR face-up on the table, you are 'Slaving' to your opponent's leads.

engine.deckDescription: A standard 52-card French deck comprising four suits: Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, and Spades. Each suit contains thirteen ranks: Ace, 2 through 10, Jack, Queen, and King, providing versatile options for various card games.
engine.suitDescription: Four traditional French suits: Hearts (Cœur), Diamonds (Carreau), Clubs (Trèfle), and Spades (Pique), each represented with standard French card iconography and distinct color coding for easy identification.
